findings.control_name: Lambda Execution Role Must Follow Least Privilege
findings.control_description: Lambda function execution roles must not have overly broad permissions. An over-privileged execution role grants the function — and any attacker who compromises or invokes it — access to AWS resources beyond what the function requires. Common violations include admin policies, wildcard resource ARNs on sensitive actions, or managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess attached to functions that only need read access to a single bucket. When combined with a public function URL or a compromised dependency, an over-privileged role converts a single function compromise into account-wide lateral movement.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 240 hours (SLA: 168 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Lambda execution role has overly broad permissions. The function can access AWS resources beyond what it requires for its intended purpose.
remediation.action: Scope the execution role policy to only the specific actions and resource ARNs the function needs. Replace managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess with inline policies scoped to specific buckets and actions. Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify unused permissions and generate a least-privilege policy from actual function activity.

fix_plan.action: Scope the execution role policy to only the specific actions and resource ARNs the function needs. Replace managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess with inline policies scoped to specific buckets and actions. Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify unused permissions and generate a least-privilege policy from actual function activity.

violation.control_name: Lambda Execution Role Must Follow Least Privilege

reasoning.clause: the compute execution role is over-privileged = true

remediation_context.action: Scope the execution role policy to only the specific actions and resource ARNs the function needs. Replace managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess with inline policies scoped to specific buckets and actions. Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify unused permissions and generate a least-privilege policy from actual function activity.

findings.defect: The Lambda function's execution role carries broader permissions than the function needs — typically an AWS-managed *FullAccess policy, a wildcard on a sensitive action, or a broadly-scoped inline policy left from development. IAM Access Analyzer would flag the role as over-privileged relative to observed call patterns.
findings.infection: Any code the function executes — intentional, injected via a compromised dependency, or triggered via a public function URL — inherits the over-privileged role's access. Lambda's assume-role happens on every invocation, so the runtime's access is the full authority of the execution role, not some subset the function happens to use. If the function is publicly invokable or called from an internet-reachable resource, this single over-privileged role converts a function compromise into lateral movement across the account.
findings.failure: Account-wide lateral movement from a single function compromise. Attacker reach extends to every AWS resource the role can touch: S3 buckets, DynamoDB tables, Secrets Manager, other Lambda functions. In a chained exploit with a compromised dependency or a public URL, this is the pivot that turns a local code-execution bug into a full data-exfiltration incident.

findings.control_name: Net Effective Permissions Must Not Include Admin-Equivalent Actions
findings.control_description: After resolving all policy layers (SCPs, permission boundaries, identity-based policies, explicit denies), a principal not designated as administrative must not have admin-equivalent effective permissions. This is distinct from CTL.IAM.POLICY.ADMIN.001 which checks policy content — this control checks the resolved effective permissions after organizational constraints are applied. A principal may have an AdminAccess policy attached but be effectively constrained by an SCP.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 240 hours (SLA: 168 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Principal has admin-equivalent net effective permissions after all policy layers are resolved.
remediation.action: Review the identity-based policies granting admin-equivalent actions. Apply an SCP or permission boundary to constrain the effective permissions. If the principal requires admin access, tag it with stave/role-type: administrative to document the intent.

fix_plan.action: Review the identity-based policies granting admin-equivalent actions. Apply an SCP or permission boundary to constrain the effective permissions. If the principal requires admin access, tag it with stave/role-type: administrative to document the intent.

violation.control_name: Net Effective Permissions Must Not Include Admin-Equivalent Actions

reasoning.clause: this identity has net-effective admin privileges = true

remediation_context.action: Review the identity-based policies granting admin-equivalent actions. Apply an SCP or permission boundary to constrain the effective permissions. If the principal requires admin access, tag it with stave/role-type: administrative to document the intent.

findings.defect: After resolving every policy layer (SCPs, permission boundaries, identity-based policies, explicit denies), this principal's net effective permissions include admin-equivalent actions such as iam:*, *:*, or a large set of high-impact actions that together equal administrative authority. The principal is not tagged as intentionally administrative.
findings.infection: Any compromise of this principal — a leaked access key, a misconfigured assume-role chain, a captured session token — yields the full admin surface. The effective-permissions resolver has already confirmed that no SCP, boundary, or deny statement constrains the admin actions at runtime, so attackers do not have to bypass organizational controls. When combined with access paths from public-facing resources (public functions, exposed IAM roles in compromised containers), admin-equivalent NEP converts one foothold into full account compromise.
findings.failure: Account-wide compromise. The attacker has the same authority as a deliberate administrator: create users, remove logging, disable guardrails, exfiltrate any resource. Containment requires organizational-level rotation and recovery, not a scoped fix.

findings.control_name: No Principal May Have Net Effective Permissions to Escalate Privileges
findings.control_description: After resolving all policy layers including transitive role assumption chains, no non-administrative principal may have effective permissions to escalate beyond their intended privilege scope. Escalation is detected in two forms: direct escalation primitives (iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachRolePolicy, etc.) in the resolved effective allow set, and transitive escalation through role chains that reach higher privilege levels than the principal's direct permissions. A developer role that can assume a pipeline role that can assume an admin role has effective admin access — neither individual role appears dangerous, but the chain is the finding.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 240 hours (SLA: 168 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Principal has effective privilege escalation capability — either a direct escalation primitive or a transitive role chain reaching admin-equivalent permissions.
remediation.action: For direct primitives: remove or scope the escalation action to specific resource ARNs. For transitive chains: remove the sts:AssumeRole grant that enables the chain, or scope it to specific non-admin role ARNs.

fix_plan.action: For direct primitives: remove or scope the escalation action to specific resource ARNs. For transitive chains: remove the sts:AssumeRole grant that enables the chain, or scope it to specific non-admin role ARNs.

violation.control_name: No Principal May Have Net Effective Permissions to Escalate Privileges

reasoning.clause: a net-effective privilege escalation path exists for this identity = true

remediation_context.action: For direct primitives: remove or scope the escalation action to specific resource ARNs. For transitive chains: remove the sts:AssumeRole grant that enables the chain, or scope it to specific non-admin role ARNs.

findings.defect: The principal's resolved net effective permissions include at least one action that enables privilege escalation — for example iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:CreateRole, iam:PassRole on an unscoped resource, or a transitive sts:AssumeRole path to a higher-privileged role. The escalation is present in the policy graph even if the individual statements don't look dangerous in isolation.
findings.infection: Any compromise of this principal becomes a compromise of every privilege the escalation path can reach. An attacker with code execution in a service running under this identity (a Lambda, an EC2 instance, a CI runner, a human-assumed role) exercises the escalation primitive and mints themselves broader credentials in a single IAM call. For direct primitives, one API call crosses the privilege boundary. For transitive chains, a short sequence of assume-role calls does the same.
findings.failure: Credential-boundary collapse. The account's intended privilege separation (dev vs. prod, service vs. admin) no longer holds for any attacker who reaches this principal. Post-incident forensics typically show a single initial compromise expanding to admin- equivalent authority within minutes of discovery.
